A 48-year-old non-smoking female with T2D complicated by neuropathy presented with right necrotizing DFU after stepping on glass 10 days prior. She had a right foot Wagner grade 3 ulcer and non-palpable pulses bilaterally. There was no HbA1C reported. An x-ray of the right foot showed soft tissue gas throughout the foot without osteomyelitis. She underwent an arterial duplex, which did not demonstrate any arterial disease; thus, an angiogram was not performed. Despite extensive debridement, she required a staged guillotine BKA and closure.

## Discussion

We describe ambulatory patients who underwent BKA/AKA from a DFU at a tertiary care center in the Bronx, NY, USA to explore their medical history, indication, and management associated with a lower extremity amputation. Our patients were young, all were Black or Hispanic, and there was marked variation in their evaluation before surgery. In addition, there is a wide variance in the care they had received before the hospitalization.

There was not a standardized battery of tests/imaging for severe DFU, likely due to differences in presentation and variation in management approaches. Ideally, the vascular status in patients with a history of DFU and risk factors should be established earlier in the disease to allow intervention, which was not the case in many patients.

Here the DFU wounds are described using the Wagner classification system, which is widely utilized for assessing DFU. However, this classification falls short in fully capturing the complexities of diabetic limb conditions that are at risk for infection, ischemia, and amputation. In contrast, the University of Texas (UT) Staging System for DFU offers a robust framework for evaluating these ulcers by emphasizing factors such as ulcer depth and the presence of infection or ischemia (4). The Wound, Ischemia, and Foot Infection (WIFi) classification system provides an even more nuanced approach by stratifying amputation risk and guiding protocols of care (5). Staging wounds using the UT classification or WIFi system may be better suited to inform a comprehensive management strategy and enhance quality improvement initiatives.

There has been a global increase in DFU-associated lower extremity amputations, despite an increased understanding of the mechanisms of ulcers, improved diagnostic capabilities, and advances in glucose control management (6). Prevention of DFU is paramount, and risk factors for diabetes-related amputations are well known, and many of them can be addressed, such as smoking cessation, screening for foot deformities – including Charcot’s arthropathy – and evaluation and management of peripheral vascular disease. In our cohort, glucose control was poor with a median HbA1c of 10.3, and insufficient glucose control increases risk of amputation in some studies (7). Screening of all patients with diabetes is an important aspect of DFU prevention. The American Diabetes Association recommends routine screening for evidence of loss of protective sensation, PAD, or foot deformity, and referral to vascular surgery if any are detected in patients with diabetes (1). Patients with a history of DFU should also routinely be referred to podiatry or vascular medicine to provide intensive foot care and reduce the high rate of recurrent ulceration and risk for amputation (8). Some patients had a delay from the time of detection of the ulcer to presenting for care, at which time tissue loss and severity of the ulcer resulted in amputation. Use of foot monitoring devices that detect pre-ulcer changes and educating patients with diabetes to call their physician for any sign of ulcer could reduce amputations due to late clinical presentation (9).

Socioeconomic status (SES) is a critical factor influencing health outcomes, hindering access to healthcare and overall patient well-being. In our cohort, patients with lower SES may have experienced delayed care due to limited access to a primary care provider, low health literacy, and lack of regular care with a podiatrist. These challenges can also contribute to suboptimal glucose control and reduced access to early vascular intervention, ultimately increasing the risk of DFU-related amputation (4).

Amputation should not be the end of intensive care for patients with DFU. To prevent the high mortality following DFU lower extremity amputation, intensive and multidisciplinary care should be offered. Furthermore, healthcare systems where amputations are performed should track health outcomes after discharge from the hospital with the goal of achieving full restoration of patients to an ambulatory state through expert rehabilitation and physical therapy.

Limitations in our study included incomplete data on patient history, such as whether they had been educated and provided the technologies/interventions to reduce the known risk factors, and the extent of prior evaluation and management to maintain foot health. Prevention and management of DFU require expertise in many fields, and the use of multidisciplinary clinics for high-risk patients to provide efficient and comprehensive care has been shown to reduce amputations, and they should be more broadly implemented (10).

This study conveys the complexities associated with DFU and associated AKA/BKA in an ethnically diverse and young group of patients in our healthcare system. Further studies on patient knowledge, provider screening, and screening technologies are underway. Enhancement in patient outreach, provider education, and implementation of a multidisciplinary clinic for high-risk patients may allow for an increase in limb salvage for our population.

## Introduction

Breast imaging-based screening leads to decreased mortality and morbidity of breast cancer [1],

as screen-detected breast cancer is more likely to be small and node negative, requiring less

extensive treatment [2]. For patients at high-risk of breast cancer, a lifetime risk of 20% or

higher, data demonstrates that earlier and augmented screening measures can significantly

decrease mortality [3]. Based on this data as well as the added yield of functional breast imaging,

most medical guidelines suggest that patients at high-risk for breast cancer consider

supplemental screening with breast MRI to enhance early detection [4-8]. To ensure timely

identification of high-risk patients, the American College of Radiology (ACR), American

Society of Breast Surgeons (ASBrS), American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

(ACOG),  National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), European Society of Breast

Imaging (EUSOBI) and the American Cancer Society (ACS) strongly recommend that all

patients be assessed for their lifetime risk of developing breast cancer [4-9]. However, some

evidence suggests that only a small percentage of high-risk patients are being identified,

prospectively assessed for risk, and undergoing recommended screening. The reason may be

multifactorial, including patients’ barriers to screening, as well as provider-level factors as both

high-risk screening guidelines and recommendation for risk assessment are inconsistent between

medical guidelines [4-6, 11, 12]. United States Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), for

instance, recommends against routine risk assessment, genetic counseling, or genetic testing for

women whose personal or family history or ancestry is not associated with potentially harmful

BRCA1/2 gene mutations [11,13]. As primary care providers (PCPs) most commonly

recommend and order breast screening studies, variability in screening based on PCPs

knowledge and medical guideline adherence may be seen. The purpose of this preliminary study

was to assess and evaluate the knowledge, attitudes, and practice patterns of primary care

physicians and advanced practice providers, at a single urban academic institution regarding

high-risk breast imaging screening and breast cancer risk assessment.

## Methods

Qualtrics XM (Provo, Utah, USA), an online survey platform, was used to anonymously assess

referring providers' knowledge of breast cancer screening guidelines and referral practices within

the institution [14].  The survey was developed based on current ACR and National

Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommendations for high-risk screening [5,6].  The

survey was sent out to providers employed by a single large academic metropolitan hospital

affiliated with a medical school with who refer patients for breast cancer screening. A total of

210 providers were contacted between July 2023 to November 2024. The survey consisted of 10

questions and assessed provider knowledge, referral practices, perceived barriers to timely

screening, and preferences in screening methods (Appendix 1). The survey was distributed via

email with a link to the online survey, and periodic reminder emails were sent to encourage

participation. Questions could be skipped, and partial surveys were accepted. Results were

analyzed in aggregate and summarized with descriptive statistics and paired T-test analysis.

## Discussion

The findings from our study provide valuable insights into the current attitudes and practices of

healthcare professionals at one institution regarding breast cancer risk assessment and high-risk

screening. Although significant appreciation of populations at higher risk of developing breast

cancer and dedication to assessing patients’ breast cancer risk was reported, there was variability

regarding age of risk assessment initiation as well as appropriate breast imaging screening

methods for those identified as high-risk. Primary care providers demonstrated an understanding

of the differences in breast cancer incidence and mortality rates among various racial and ethnic

groups. The majority correctly identified non-Hispanic white women as having the highest

incidence rates, most, 96% (47/49), recognized that non-Hispanic black women face the highest

mortality rates from breast cancer [15]. This understanding is crucial for developing targeted

screening and intervention strategies for at-risk populations. Additionally, identifying Ashkenazi

Jewish women as a high-risk group for breast cancer underscores the importance of culturally

competent healthcare practices that consider genetic factors.

Nearly all the respondents, 98% (47/49) reported assessing their patients’ risk of breast cancer,

with the majority 55% (27/49) doing so most of the time or always. However, there was a

significantly variable understanding in the appropriate breast screening methods for those

assessed as high-risk, with two of the primary care provider respondents (4%) self-professing

lack of knowledge of the appropriate imaging. Evidently, there is a need for continued education


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

through grand rounds, consultation services, or webinars, to enhance knowledge among referring

providers. Breast MRI has consistently been shown to have superior sensitivity for breast cancer,

predominately detecting smaller, node-negative and more aggressive cancers than

mammography alone [16, 17]. Therefore, supplemental breast MRI screening is recommended

for women with a high lifetime risk for the development of breast cancer (≥ 20%) by the ACS,

NCCN, ACR, ASBrS, ACOG and EUSOBI [4-9]. Yet, as also demonstrated by our study, there

is still underutilization of this screening breast imaging modality in high-risk patients [18].

Underutilization of MRI may be attributed to several factors, including lack of familiarity with

guidelines among providers and patients, cost and insurance barriers, patient hesitancy toward

MRI as it may be anxiety inducing, and challenges in access and availability, particularly in rural

and underserved areas [19].

Women with a BRCA1 mutation face a lifetime breast cancer risk of approximately 55-72%,

while those with a BRCA2 mutation have a 45-69% risk [20]. This contrasts sharply with the

general population, where the lifetime breast cancer risk is approximately 12–13% [21].

Moreover, breast cancer mortality is significantly higher in high-risk populations when

appropriate screening is delayed or omitted, with BRCA carriers often developing cancer at

younger ages and with more aggressive tumor subtypes, such as triple-negative breast cancer

[22].


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

Furthermore, despite providing regular risk assessment to their patients, primary care providers

at our institution highlighted several barriers to their ability to do this routinely. Although time

limitations were most reported by 20% (8/40), other barriers were reported nearly as frequently,

including a lack of knowledge about available assessment tools, limited access to these tools, and

concerns about downstream costs. This suggests a multifactorial barrier in the clinical workflow

to providing the standard of care routine risk assessment. Record et al, found similar challenges

faced by family practice, OB/GYN and those who work in an academic setting, with time being

the largest reported barrier, and education as the second most identified barrier [23]. It is

important that radiology departments, specifically breast radiologists, in institutions across the

country provide the necessary education, through grand rounds, multidisciplinary conferences,

team meetings and webinars to educate providers ordering supplemental screening for high-risk

patients, similar to the ASBrS, which has extensive experience producing education activities to

educate surgeons regarding risk-assessment and the role of genetic testing [24]. Furthermore, this

approach should be in collaboration with other national groups including the ACR and SBI. A

review by Borgquist et al, reaffirms the need for adequate risk assessment tools, a consensus on

the definition of high-risk and the need for more information on risk perception and

communication [25].

Finally, there was a strong consensus among respondents in regard to assessing all individuals

assigned female at birth for their lifetime breast cancer risk by age 25-30 indicating a growing


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

recognition of the value of early risk assessment, which aligns with most contemporary

guidelines advocating for proactive screening measures. Nonetheless, more than a quarter of

respondents did not agree with the statement that all women should be assessed for lifetime risk

of breast cancer by age 25-30, likely secondary to self-reported adherence to different medical

guidelines. Variations exist among screening guidelines for high-risk patients from the various

societies; for instance the USPSTF does not recommend early risk assessment or screening with

breast MRI for high-risk patients, except those with elevated cancer risk associated with BRCA

gene mutations [11], whereas the NCCN, ACS, ASBrS, ACR, EUSOBI and ACOG recommend

early risk assessment and annual screening mammogram in addition to annual screening breast

MRI [4-9]. It is inevitable that conflicting guidelines contribute to provider variation in

implementing risk assessments and recommending additional screening tools, such as breast

MRI for high-risk patients [26].

A substantial proportion of disagreement originated from providers with more than 21 years of

experience, suggesting that more experienced clinicians may be less inclined to adopt newer

recommendations due to entrenched clinical practices or differing interpretations of emerging

evidence. For example, they may be less comfortable adopting, or may simply be unaware of,

newer recommendations for early risk assessment. The agreement of participants in the survey

with experience of 11-20 years may suggest that mid-career level physicians are more well-

informed and up to date on newer recommendations. Educational outreach to clinicians in the


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

later stages of their careers might be helpful in increasing the number of patients who benefit

from early risk assessment. Additionally, a significant percentage of OB/GYNs agreed that

patients should be assessed for lifetime breast cancer risk by ages 25-30, as compared to other

health care providers, suggesting that OB/GYNs have educational tools and willingness to adopt

newer guidelines. We should further examine the experiences of OB/GYNs to help educate other

health care providers.

Ensuring that referring physicians are informed about current risk assessment and high-risk

screening guidelines is essential not only for improving patient outcomes but also for reducing

disparities in access to evidence-based care. Our survey highlights the variability in practice

patterns among primary care providers, even within the same institution. Variable approaches to

risk assessment and breast cancer screening recommendations seen from their medical providers

may lead to confusion, unequal access, and ultimate nonadherence to recommendations by

patients. Moreover, the consequences of inconsistent screening practices are likely to

disproportionately affect Black and African American women, who already face significant

disparities in breast cancer outcomes. Breast cancer mortality rates are 40% higher among Black

and African American women compared to White and European American women, despite

similar incidence rates [23]. Additionally, Black and African American women are more likely

to be diagnosed with aggressive breast cancer subtypes—such as estrogen receptor-negative and

triple-negative breast cancer—before the age of 50, a trend also observed in Ashkenazi Jewish


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

women [28]. These disparities are compounded by systemic barriers to healthcare access,

delayed diagnoses, and lower rates of guideline-concordant care. While Black and African

American women have a higher prevalence of BRCA genetic mutations, they are less likely to

receive genetic testing and risk assessment services [29]. Ensuring that Black and African

American women, along with other at-risk populations, receive timely risk assessments and

appropriate breast cancer screening based on the latest guidelines is essential for addressing the

longstanding disparities in breast cancer screening and outcomes.

Despite the valuable insights this study provides, it is essential to acknowledge its limitations.

The small sample size of 49 respondents from a single institution limits the generalizability of

these findings to broader populations and settings. Additionally, the reliance on self-reported

data may introduce bias, as participants could overstate their adherence to guidelines or the

frequency of their practices. The cross-sectional design of the survey further limits the ability to

draw definitive conclusions about the relationships between awareness, practices, and patient

outcomes. Moreover, the survey design, including the structure of questions on supplemental

screening, may have contributed to misinterpretations or incomplete responses. This highlights

the need for more robust, multi-institutional studies.

## Conclusion

While this study demonstrates a clear commitment among healthcare providers to assess breast

cancer risk and make appropriate referrals, it also highlights the need for continued education

and training due to variable knowledge and practice patterns. Variability in knowledge and

practice patterns among referring providers within the same institution underscores this need.

Enhancing providers' awareness of ancillary screening recommendations for high-risk groups,

particularly Black and Ashkenazi Jewish women, can promote timely intervention and treatment,

potentially reducing mortality rates in these populations. Moving forward, future research should

evaluate the effectiveness of targeted educational initiatives aimed at improving healthcare

providers' understanding of breast cancer risk assessment and appropriate imaging

recommendations.

# Abstract

Epithelial sheath neuroma is a cutaneous tumor presenting as an erythematous and often painful lesion on the skin of the back. We report a 74-year-old woman with a 7mm epithelial sheath neuroma located on the right upper central back. The initial clinical impression was a basal cell carcinoma and histopathologically, the tumor mimicked a carcinoma with perineural invasion. She had no prior trauma or surgeries at the surgical site. She reported experiencing pain at the site of the tumor. Pain is a symptom of more than half of the reported epithelial sheath neuroma cases. The papule was excised, and there has been no recurrence at the surgical site. We report the unusual occurrence of this very uncommon neoplasm, a tumor that might be inadvertently confused with an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma.

## Introduction

Epithelial sheath neuroma (ESN) is an extremely uncom­ mon tumor containing both neural and epithelial ele­ ments. ESN typically presents as an erythematous papule or plaque on the upper or mid back. The pathogenesis of an ESN is unknown; however, it has been suggested that ESN stems from an abnormal reactive hyperplasia of the peripheral nerves and epithelium.1 Uncommon traits of ESN include that it has only been reported on the skin of the back and is disproportionately prevalent (3:1) among elderly women.2 Management of this condition includes simple excision.3 We describe a case of an ESN in an el­ derly woman with chronic back pain.

## Case Synopsis

A 74-year-old woman with a history of basal and squa­ mous cell carcinoma presented for a full body skin exam­

ination with a painful growth she found on her back. Her past medical history included perforated and bleeding ulcers, hypothyroidism, and hypertension; these comor­ bidities were receiving appropriate medical treatment. On examination, she had multiple brown, evenly pig­ mented macules/papules on her trunk and extremities.

The full body skin exam revealed a pink scaly, erythe­ matous papule on her right upper central back measur­ ing 7mm (Figure 1). The patient reported that the lesion was very painful. The clinical impression was concerning for a basal cell carcinoma or other nonmelanoma skin cancer. A shave biopsy was performed. The biopsy re­ vealed a squamous proliferative lesion without superfi­ cial connection to the epidermis (Figure 2). There were multiple peripheral small nerve structures that were sheathed by mature squamous epithelium (Figures 3-5). The histopathologic findings were diagnostic of an ESN. There were no instances of previous trauma, surgical in­ terventions, or skin disorders documented at the site. The ESN was excised. The patient followed up nineteen days post procedure and has had several visits there­ after, with no regrowth of the lesion.

## Discussion

Epithelial sheath neuroma is an uncommon cutaneous benign tumor named by Requena et al in 2000.4 Four­ teen cases of ESN have been documented in literature to date. Notably, ESN can imitate the perineural invasion (PNI) associated with aggressive squamous cell carcino­ mas (SCC). However, ESN stands apart from carcinoma­ tous PNI owing to the presence of an elevated number of enlarged nerve fibers and the lack of cytologic atypia of the individual epithelial elements.3 Additionally, the ab­ sence of prior malignancy further supports the diagnosis of ESN and mitigates against the possibility of carcinoma­ tous perineural invasion.5 These histological distinctions are crucial for accurate diagnosis of patients with ESN. ## Conclusion

Our case report demonstrates the importance of differ­ entiating ESN from other malignancies with PNI, such as aggressive SCCs and the infiltrative, micronodular, and

squamous variants of basal cell carcinoma. The presence of enlarged nerve fibers and the absence of cytologic atypia are features that distinguish ESN from carcinoma­ tous perineural invasion. This case highlights the need for consideration of ESN in the differential diagnosis of lesions exhibiting PNI.
